Ok, I get it. But, what's the point? Is it purely fanservice? Just a sexy show that is meant to get you off but also include giant mecha?

No.

Darling in the Franxxx, in my estimation at least, is a meaningful show that provides us with an interesting insight into modern-day Japan. Let me explain what I mean.

Japan's Population Problem

In order to understand any work of art, we need to think about the culture it originates from. So, what's going on in Japan right now? Let's take a look at this graph. See all that shrinking at the bottom? That's not what you want. That's what you see in populations that are collapsing because they aren't reproducing at replacement rates. Ultimately, this could lead to a population crisis: as the general bulk of the citizenry become older, and start to exit the workforce, there is nobody to replace them. This becomes disastrous to the economy, as companies begin to actually wind down their operations simply because they can't find anybody to hire. As people grow older, they need care--but you can't provide that care unless you have a thriving economy that produces medical supplies, food, infrastructure and so on. None of this is achievable when only, say, a third or less of your population is below the age of 50.

Japan is not populated by idiots. They can see the writing on the wall, and their government agencies are aware that this is a problem:

  • They're providing greater incentives to have kids.
  • Entire villages and rural areas are abandoned, simply because there are no young people to move in after the old inhabitants died.
  • Some prefectures have considered providing sabotaged condoms to citizens!

Why are Japanese people not having children? Well, you can talk about things like the high cost of raising a child, the fact that children born out of wedlock are legally disenfranchised compared to 'legitimate' kids, and other factors, but I'd like to focus on a specific issue that Japan has faced: Salaryman Culture, and the death of romance.

What is a Salaryman?

We see show after show after show about high school kids in Japan, and they always are working their asses off on their grades despite piloting mechs, staying awake through 'the dark hour' to fight monsters, turning into magical girls, or what-the-fuck-ever. Why? Because you are set on a track that you cannot meaningfully alter when you graduate college.

You go to grade school, and your grades then determine a bit about where you go to high school. Your high school career ends with entrance exams. Your scores on entrance exams determine where you go to college. As you near the end of college, a company selects you for employment. And that's that--you are employed by that company for the remainder of your LIFE. Quitting a job is to exit the workforce entirely, there's no such thing as "changing jobs". You will receive promotions over time, guaranteed. If you suck at your job, you will be promoted into teams of other fuck-ups that are paid, but never given anything too important to do, because it's know that you'll fuck it up.

Your company is expected to take care of you for your entire life. This is easy to see when you look at what it takes to fire somebody in Japan. The perception is that the company is literally turning someone out onto the streets to die. The government gets involved, you need to demonstrate SEVERE misconduct on the employee's behalf in order to get them the hell out.

So, when you are employed, what can you look forward to?

  • Thirteen hour days
  • Six day weeks
  • REQUIRED social activities after work
  • Scant vacation time, close to none at all.

It's expected that you will get to work by six or seven in the morning, work all day, your boss will take your department out for drinks, you'll leave at 11pm or so to catch the last train home, kiss your wife goodnight, and then do it all again the next day. Six days a week. UNTIL YOUR SIXTIES.

But at least you have Sunday. You have one day a week that you can spend nurturing that relationship with your wife at home, right? WRONG. Social events outside of work with your department, organized by the head of your department, often are scheduled during your day off. You are considered antisocial and are putting your career at tremendous risk by not attending these events.

So, WHY would we get married at all? What's the point? There is no room for romance. Your wife probably can remember your name, and she certainly sleeps next to you in bed, but she basically will never see you and you won't see her. All you'll really know is that she has access to your bank account and that by working as you do, you are taking care of her.

In this context, I believe it's easy to understand why there is a complete collapse of young people's interest in marriage and family. Would YOU feel comfortable picking a close friend in your 20's, and then saying to them, "Here's my debit card. I'm never really going to see you again, but take good care of yourself, ok"? It's just an expense. There's no reward in it except, honestly, a sense of fulfillment of duty: by having kids, you've helped the population of the country along. But that's about it.

Darling in the Franxxx

So let's bring this all back around to the show. Warning: Mild Spoilers!!

I believe that Darling in the Franxxx imagines a world where the population is aged, technology-addicted, and still bought-in to the idea that life only really exists to be applied to things that are useful. It's the "burn out" state that Japan is sortof in right now. We see some adults, but they're old; the relationships are sexless and seem pretty loveless as well. We see an elderly man with a big wide grin on his face as his brain is stimulated into bathing itself in dopamine without him having any real sort of experience to justify it.

By contrast, Squad 13's life is vibrant, and their struggles are powerful and impactful. They are experiencing interpersonal relationships in a deep and profound way, and the pervy old doctor is "the guy who gets it". He knows that you have to experience happiness with your peers, and most of all, with your body. Our crew are going through puberty, and learning what a 'kiss' is. The Franxxx is just a metaphor for a functional relationship: it doesn't work when partners are not "on the same wavelength". It feels great when it works. It involves vulnerability, the sharing of minds, and yes, sex. What is sex to humans, after all? It defies intellectualizing, it can't be abstracted into cold, calculated, logical ideas. You have to get the pussy wet, you have to get the penis erect. These reactions are no more voluntary, no more available to the cold, calculating, logical mind than the shedding of tears or the secretion of adrenaline.

In Conclusion

And so, while the sex metaphors are over the top, I think it's absolutely justified and understandable. Darling in the Franxxx is a sincere attempt to remind the population of Japan that love, and sex, feel good--and that life is more worth living if you experience them.
